The Model as a Function of Parameters and Data

Source: R/report.R
loglik.Rd

Turn a fitted model back into a function. loglik(), gradient() and hessian() evaluate the model's log-likelihood and its first two derivatives at coefficients and data of the caller's choosing, so a fit can be profiled, differenced or handed to a user-written optimizer.

If only the fit is given, these functions evaluate the model at the fitted coefficients and on the fitting data.

Usage

loglik(object, par = NULL, data = NULL, ...)

gradient(object, par = NULL, data = NULL, ...)

hessian(
  object,
  par = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  information = distributions7::observed_info(),
  ...
)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

par

A named list of coefficient vectors, each as long as the design of the equation that it names. A distribution parameter that the list omits keeps its fitted coefficients, so a list may change one equation and leave the others at the fit. Defaults to the fitted coefficients. A par that is not a named list, a name that is not a distribution parameter, or a vector of the wrong length is an error. The own parameters of a structural term are not among the arguments.

data

A data frame with the columns that the model names. Defaults to the data used to fit the model. New data must carry the response, since a likelihood needs one.

...

Passed to methods. The shipped methods do not read it.

information

hessian() only: the matrix whose negative is returned, an object that inherits from distributions7::Information. distributions7::observed_info() (the default) gives the Hessian of the log-likelihood at the data, and distributions7::expected_info() gives minus the Fisher information, whose method selects how the expectation is obtained. auto_info() is not accepted. The default is distributions7::observed_info(), whatever the family, because the result is a Hessian and not a variance; the variance objects resolve a NULL information by the family (see information_objects).

Value

loglik() gives a single number. gradient() gives a named list of numeric vectors, one per distribution parameter. hessian() gives a symmetric p x p matrix over the stacked regression coefficients, where p is their total count. The own parameters of a structural term are not among them and have no entry in the gradient or in the Hessian.

The name

The generic is loglik, not logLik. R's stats::logLik() returns the log-likelihood of a fitted model and carries df and nobs with it, and overloading it would give one name two behaviors. Both functions are available, and loglik(fit) with no further arguments equals logLik(fit), which checks that the callable route and the fitting route evaluate the same model.

Generics instead of closures

A closure captures its environment, which here means the data. A fit carrying one would hold the frame twice and would keep a stale copy after the data changed.

The generics rebuild from the specification that the fit keeps whole, running each term's blueprint against data by the same path as predict.StatmodFit(). A factor's levels, a spline's knots and a basis reparametrization are therefore reapplied to the new rows and not estimated again.

Likelihood without the penalty

All three functions evaluate the likelihood without the penalty. The penalized objective at given coefficients is a different quantity, and the hyperparameters are not arguments of these functions.

See also

logLik.StatmodFit() for the log-likelihood of the fit with its degrees of freedom, vcov.StatmodFit() for the variance matrix, predict.StatmodFit() for the same reapplication on new data.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(40))
dd$y <- 1 + dd$x + rnorm(40, sd = 0.5)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)

# At the fitted coefficients it equals the conditional log-likelihood.
all.equal(loglik(fit), as.numeric(logLik(fit)))
#> [1] TRUE

# Far from the fit it is lower, and the gradient gives the direction of
# increase.
loglik(fit, par = list(mu = c(0, 0), sigma = 0))
#> [1] -88.88139
gradient(fit, par = list(mu = c(0, 0), sigma = 0))
#> $mu
#> [1] 61.90424 34.21924
#> 
#> $sigma
#> [1] 64.2477
#> 

# The gradient with respect to the mu coefficients vanishes at the fit.
# The sigma coordinate is estimated on the REML criterion, so its
# component is minus the number of mu coefficients (here -2).
gradient(fit)
#> $mu
#> [1] 1.953993e-14 6.217249e-15
#> 
#> $sigma
#> [1] -2
#> 

# The observed information is positive definite at the fit.
eigen(-hessian(fit), only.values = TRUE)$values
#> [1] 294.47910  76.00000  13.73987
